headline: Oura reportedly eyeing $16B+ IPO as soon as September, seeking $3B funding
summary: Oura, the smart ring maker, is reportedly planning a U.S. IPO next month, aiming to raise up to $3 billion and achieve a valuation exceeding $16 billion. This marks a significant increase from its $10.9 billion valuation last year.
details: Smart ring maker Oura is reportedly preparing for a U.S. IPO as early as September, aiming to raise up to $3 billion. Sources suggest the offering could value the company at over $16 billion, a substantial figure for the wearable tech firm. Investors are also expected to sell a significant portion of their stock.

This potential valuation represents a major leap from Oura's $10.9 billion valuation in September last year. That round saw the company close an $875 million Series E, backed by prominent investors like Fidelity and ICONIQ.

Oura faces competition from rivals like Samsung's Galaxy Ring and fitness band maker Whoop. Like Whoop, Oura has expanded its market, moving from a niche in biohacking to a broader sleep-and-recovery brand.

The company confidentially filed for an IPO in May. Oura has projected revenues of $500 million for 2024, $1 billion for 2025, and nearly $2 billion for 2026, though full financial details await its public S-1 filing.

Despite its growth, Oura is also facing a proposed class action lawsuit in San Francisco. The suit alleges the company misleads consumers about the accuracy of its sleep tracking features, claiming it measures sleep stages which typically require clinical settings.

Oura has issued a statement to TechCrunch, refuting the lawsuit's claims. A spokesperson stated the company plans to defend itself, asserting that Oura's sleep staging has been validated in multiple studies against polysomnography, the gold standard.

headline_marked: [[Apple reverses Hide My Email domain change]] after user pushback, keeping addresses on icloud.com
headline: Apple reverses Hide My Email domain change after user pushback, keeping addresses on icloud.com
summary: Apple will no longer move iCloud+ Hide My Email addresses to a new domain, reversing a decision made just two months ago following significant user feedback. This means existing aliases will remain on the familiar icloud.com domain.
details: Apple has officially reversed its decision to move iCloud+ Hide My Email addresses from the icloud.com domain. This change comes just two months after the initial announcement, following considerable user feedback and concerns.

The original plan would have transitioned all new and existing Hide My Email aliases to a different, less familiar domain. This sparked worries among users about potential confusion and the perceived loss of consistency for their privacy-focused email addresses.

With this reversal, all iCloud+ Hide My Email addresses will continue to be generated and function under the icloud.com domain. This ensures continuity and addresses the privacy and branding concerns raised by the user community.
